beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing is about context, skills, output or an interface, and the hard part is whether people take it up.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: nothing new. I already have an example: our CRM dashboards.

beats.trigger: **Name** the likely adoption failure before it happens, including the social failure that's hardest to see
beats.got: nothing new. It is a list of five verbs.

beats.trigger: And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: I hesitate because my team would use it without my judgment on the churn article.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from the teammate's job, not from my tool.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: There is a clear test for whether the job statement is specific enough. I can use that on any brief.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Pick the sharing form for the outcome, not for the infrastructure.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new. It is a handoff line.

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it
beats.got: The next step is finding what will block uptake.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Find the one blocker that explains the others and fix that first. Mine is probably that we have no shared home for context files.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: My team's plan will look finished technically and have empty people boxes. That is where I'm actually stuck.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure
beats.got: nothing new. It is a transition.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: Treat the plans as guesses to test, not as a rollout.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: Ask what would make a person drop their current way of working. That is a better question than 'how do I get adoption?'

beats.trigger: one person, one question about how they do the job today, and one selected assumption with its test.
beats.got: The output is one conversation and one test I can run next week.

beats.trigger: Test the switch, not the solution.
beats.got: A four-step habit I can reuse on any rollout.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: A candidate that does not move it is not a candidate.
beats.got: nothing new. This repeats the exercise.

beats.trigger: Hand someone the agent file and they run it, get a generic answer, and quietly stop.
beats.got: The agent file is just instructions. The value is in the memory and corrections, so a copy gives a generic result.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily. The person who answers for the output does not, and my CFO will ask who that is.

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: The interface depends on other people's availability.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A good agent-built analysis still stalled, because leadership had not done the work themselves and the urgency had moved on. That could happen to my pricing pilot.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: nothing new. It is the big idea again in other words.

beats.trigger: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: People take things up when they resemble something they already do. It's a bit abstract for me.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: The conditions for switching are small and specific, and a trusted peer going first is one of them.

beats.trigger: A missing name is a finding
beats.got: An empty name field shows what isn't built yet. Start with one person.

take_homes: Don't hand over the agent. Hand over the context, the checks, and a named person who answers for the output.
Start from what my teammate is trying to get done and what they use today. Ask what would have to be true for them to switch.
An empty name in the people plan is the real finding. Our missing shared home for context files is probably the bottleneck.

monday.move: Ask one person on my team how they build the pilot-cohort brief today, and test one assumption: they will use the shared context file if it sits where they already look. I'll also put the context files in one shared place and rerun the brief with fresh data.
monday.who: The pricing analyst on my team, then the pricing working group for the brief itself.
monday.when: Monday morning for the conversation, and the rerun brief goes out by Wednesday.
monday.stop_condition: If the analyst keeps using their private copy after two tries, I stop and ask why instead of pushing it.
monday.blocker: We have no shared place for the context files and everyone keeps their own copy. The owner of that place is unassigned.

misconception.why: I still think prompts matter. But the point that the work lives in the memory and the corrections, and that a copied agent file gives a generic answer, made me see that better prompts won't get fourteen people working the same way.

one_line: Less about AI than about why my team won't use what I build. The first half is a bit repetitive, but the 'name one person' idea is useful.
